sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve that rises, overshoots, and then settles.
sections.body_md:
A second-order system has two poles. Two numbers place them. The natural frequency \(\omega_n\) is the distance from the origin to either pole, and it sets the speed of the motion. The damping ratio \(\zeta\) is the cosine of the angle from the negative real axis to the pole, and it decides whether the motion rings.

When \(\zeta<1\) the poles are a complex conjugate pair and the free motion oscillates inside a decaying envelope. When \(\zeta=1\) the poles are real and equal, which is critical damping. When \(\zeta>1\) the poles are real and distinct, which is overdamped, and the motion does not ring. The formulas that turn \(\zeta\) into a percent overshoot, a peak time, or a settling time belong to the step-response specifications, not to this placement.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Standard form, with a unit DC gain:
\[
\ddot y + 2\zeta\omega_n\dot y + \omega_n^2 y = \omega_n^2 u.
\]
For \(\zeta<1\) the poles are \(-\zeta\omega_n \pm j\omega_d\) with \(\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\). The real part is \(-\zeta\omega_n\). Critical damping is the repeated pole \(-\omega_n\). Overdamping splits that pole into two different negative real numbers whose product is \(\omega_n^2\) and whose sum is \(2\zeta\omega_n\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(\omega_n=7\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\zeta=0.25\). The real part of each pole is \(-\zeta\omega_n=-7\times 0.25=-1.75\). The damped frequency is
\[
\omega_d=7\sqrt{1-0.0625}=7\sqrt{0.9375}=6.778\ \mathrm{rad/s}.
\]
The poles are \(-1.75\pm j6.778\). Because \(\zeta\) is below 1, the pair is underdamped. Calling 6.778 the natural frequency uses the imaginary part. Calling the magnitude 1.75 the natural frequency uses only that real part. The distance from the origin is 7, and that is \(\omega_n\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The natural frequency is the distance from the origin, not the ringing frequency. The ringing frequency is \(\omega_d\), which is smaller than \(\omega_n\) whenever \(\zeta>0\). Critical damping is \(\zeta=1\), not the overdamped case. Overdamping is \(\zeta>1\), two distinct real poles. A sign error that puts the pair in the right half-plane is an unstable system, not a lightly damped one.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Step-response specifications turn \(\zeta\) and \(\omega_n\) into rise time, overshoot, and settling time. A series RLC circuit writes the same \(\zeta\) as \(1/(2Q)\) next to its resonant frequency. A mass, a damper, and a spring are the same two numbers, with \(\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\zeta=b/(2\sqrt{km})\).
